summary.heading: Stage 2: Why call it God? Immutability, eternity, immateriality
summary.body:
Stage 2 argues that the undeniable reality of change entails the existence of **God**. There are two reasons for using that name. First, the unactualized actualizer is the ultimate cause of things in the most intimate sense possible: it is what **keeps them in existence** at every moment they exist. Whatever else God is supposed to be, he is the ultimate cause of things. Second, the defining attributes of God as traditionally conceived **follow** from pure actuality. Feser gives only a sketch here and promises a full chapter on the divine attributes later.

- **Immutability.** Being purely actual and so without potentiality, the cause cannot go from potential to actual — it cannot change.
- **Eternity.** Existing in time entails being changeable, so an immutable cause must be eternal in the strong sense of existing **outside time altogether**: it neither begins nor ends but simply is, timelessly.
- **Immateriality and incorporeality.** Being material entails being changeable and in time, so an immutable, eternal cause must be immaterial and have no body of any kind.

summary.heading: Perfection and goodness
summary.body:
What is it for something to be imperfect? A squirrel hit by a car may be unable to escape predators as quickly as it needs to; a tree with damaged roots may be unstable or unable to draw in enough water and nutrients. Such a defect is what philosophers traditionally call a **privation**: the absence of something a thing’s nature requires for completeness — a failure to realize a potential built into it. A thing is perfect, then, to the extent that it has realized such potentials and is free of privation. Something purely actual has no unrealized potential and no privation at all, so it has **maximal perfection**.

Goodness works the same way. In a general sense, a thing is good to the extent that it realizes the potentials inherent in the kind of thing it is, and bad insofar as it fails to. A good painter has actualized his potential for mastering craftsmanship, composition and the rest; a bad painter has failed to acquire those skills. A purely actual cause, having no unactualized potential, cannot be deficient in any way. It is perfect, and so **fully good**.

summary.heading: Unity: there can be only one purely actual cause
summary.body:
Could there be more than one purely actual cause? Not even in principle. There can be two or more things of a kind only if something **differentiates** them — some feature one has and another lacks. We usually tell things apart by material or temporal features: one is bigger, taller, earlier or later than another. But what is purely actual is immaterial and eternal, so no such features are available.

More generally, members of a kind are differentiated by some perfection or privation that one has and the other lacks: this tree’s roots are sturdier than that one’s; this squirrel has lost its tail and that one hasn’t. But what is purely actual has no privation at all and is maximally perfect, so there is nothing in principle to distinguish one purely actual cause from another. Hence the attribute of **unity**: there is exactly one purely actual cause, and it is the same one unactualized actualizer to which all things owe their existence.

summary.heading: Omnipotence
summary.body:
To have **power** is simply to be able to make something happen — to actualize some potential. The cause of the existence of all things is not just one actual thing among others; it is pure actuality itself, and it is the **source of all the actualizing power** anything else has (every actualization either comes from it directly or from a series that terminates in it). A being from which all power derives has all possible power. It is **omnipotent**.

Feser sums up the results so far: the purely actual actualizer is the one, immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent and fully good cause that keeps all things in being from moment to moment. Can we go further and attribute something **personal**, like intelligence? Yes — but first we need an account of what intelligence is and a further principle about cause and effect.

summary.heading: What intelligence is
summary.body:
On the traditional view, intelligence involves three capacities:

1. Grasping **abstract or universal concepts** — for example, the concept *man*, which you have when you know not just this or that man but what it is to be a man at all, a concept that applies to every possible man, not only existing ones.
2. Combining concepts into **complete thoughts** — as in the thought that all men are mortal.
3. **Reasoning** from some thoughts to others — as in inferring that Socrates is mortal from the premises that all men are mortal and that Socrates is a man.

The first is the most fundamental, since thoughts and inferences are built from concepts.

To have a concept is to have in the mind a **form or pattern** — the very same form that exists in the things you think about. All men share a form that makes them men; all triangles share a form that makes them triangles. When such a form is realized in matter, you get an individual man or an individual triangle. When you think about men or triangles in general, you abstract from all the particulars and grasp what is common. That is the essence of intellectual activity: **having the form of a thing without being that kind of thing**. A material triangle has triangularity by *being* a triangle; you have triangularity in your mind without *becoming* a triangle.

summary.heading: The principle of proportionate causality: the $20 gift
summary.body:
Two principles about cause and effect are now on the table. The first is the **principle of causality**: whenever something is changed or caused to exist, a potential is actualized, and something already actual actualizes it. The second is the **principle of proportionate causality**: whatever is in an effect must in some way be in its cause, though not necessarily in the same way — because a cause cannot give what it does not have.

Feser illustrates with a gift of $20. I can cause you to have $20 only if I have it to give, but there are many ways of ‘having’ it. I might have a $20 bill in my wallet, or two tens, or four fives. I might have nothing in my wallet but $20 in the bank and write you a check, or borrow it, or earn it. More fancifully, I might have a friend with access to the Treasury’s printing press, or even persuade Congress to let me print my own twenties. If none of those ways is open to me, I cannot give you $20.

These illustrate three traditional modes:

- **Formally**: I have a $20 bill in hand — I already instantiate the very pattern (having a twenty) that I cause you to instantiate.
- **Virtually**: I don’t have the bill on hand but have the power to obtain it (bank credit).
- **Eminently**: I have the higher power to bring twenty-dollar bills into existence in the first place (my Congress-granted license to print).

So the principle says what is in the effect must be in the cause at least virtually or eminently, even if not formally.

summary.heading: Intelligence and omniscience derived
summary.body:
Now apply this to the purely actual cause. It is the cause of the existence of **everything that exists or could exist**. But to cause something to exist is always to cause something **of a particular kind** — a stone rather than a tree, a tree rather than a cat — that is, something bearing a certain form or pattern. So this cause is the cause of every possible form or pattern. By proportionate causality, these forms must somehow be **in** the cause. And they must be there in a fully **universal or abstract** way, since the cause is the source of *every possible* instance of each form, not just this or that one. But having forms in a universal, abstract way is precisely the fundamental capacity of **intellect**.

Further, the cause accounts not only for things but for **how they are related** — not only for men but for its being true that all men are mortal; not only for this cat but for this cat’s being on this mat. So these effects too must pre-exist in the cause, in a way involving the combination of forms — that is, the way **thoughts** exist in us. What exists in created things thus pre-exists in their cause much as the things we make pre-exist in our minds as ideas or plans. They exist in the cause **virtually and eminently**, not formally: the cause is not itself a cat or a tree (it can’t be — it is immaterial), but it can cause cats and trees and anything else.

Finally, since there is nothing that exists or could exist that falls outside the range of this intelligent cause’s thoughts, it is **omniscient**. Feser closes Stage 2 by noting that far more could be said, and will be in the later chapter on the divine attributes, but that this sketch already shows the cause of things answers to the traditional description of God.

summary.heading: The formal statement: a 50-step argument
summary.body:
After a short recap — change is undeniable; it requires potentials actualized by something already actual; linear series might run back forever, but their members depend at every moment on hierarchical series that must end in a purely actual actualizer of existence; and such a cause must have the key divine attributes, so that things can exist at any moment only if God sustains them — Feser restates everything as a numbered, 50-step argument. The steps fall into clear blocks:

- **Steps 1–14**: from the reality of change, through the principle of causality and the existence of a changing substance, to a hierarchical series of concurrent actualizers of existence that cannot regress infinitely — so there is a purely actual actualizer.
- **Steps 15–18**: unity.
- **Steps 19–27**: immutability, eternity, immateriality, incorporeality.
- **Steps 28–32**: perfection and full goodness.
- **Steps 33–37**: omnipotence.
- **Steps 38–47**: intelligence and omniscience, via the principle of proportionate causality.
- **Steps 48–50**: such a cause is what it is for God to exist; so God exists.

(See the Argument tab for every step restated with its justification.)

summary.heading: Objections: the ‘first cause isn’t God’ complaint
summary.body: Feser acknowledges that the derivation of the divine attributes rests on philosophical assumptions that will be controversial, and he promises to address them at length later. The point here was to show that the Aristotelian argument goes **far beyond** a bare cause of change. That alone undercuts a common but ungrounded objection: that first-cause arguments could never tell us enough about the first cause to identify it with God. Other objections to first-cause arguments in general are postponed to a later chapter devoted to them. What the rest of this chapter tackles are objections aimed at the **distinctively Aristotelian** features of the argument.

summary.heading: Common misunderstandings (1): beginnings and the universe as a whole
summary.body:
Some objections look obvious and even fatal but rest on basic misreadings.

**The ‘beginning of the universe’ misreading.** Readers are so used to thinking of God as the cause of the universe’s beginning that they read this idea even into an argument that explicitly rejects it, and then ask how we could know the universe had a beginning. But Feser said all along that even if the universe, or a series of universes, extends infinitely into the past, that is **irrelevant**. The claim is that for things to exist here and now — at any moment they exist — they must be **sustained** in existence here and now by God.

**The ‘whole universe’ misreading.** Others think the argument assumes the universe as a whole must have a cause and then object that even if each part has a cause, the whole needn’t. But no premise of the argument concerns the universe as a whole. The argument starts with **any single, trivial thing** existing now — a stone, a cup of coffee — and shows that even it requires a purely actual cause actualizing it at this moment. Feser does say that this applies to everything, and so to the universe as a whole — but that is a **consequence** of the argument, not a premise.

summary.heading: Common misunderstandings (2): ‘What caused God?’
summary.body:
The most famous stock objection: if everything has a cause, what caused God? And if God can be uncaused, why not other things? The argument, it’s said, commits **special pleading**.

Feser gives two replies. First, the argument **never says** ‘everything has a cause’. It says any change requires a cause — more precisely, that **whatever goes from potential to actual** has a cause. Second, the exception for God is **not arbitrary**. Other things need causes precisely because they have potentials needing actualization. What is purely actual has no potential, so there is nothing in it that needs to be — or even could be — actualized. It is the one thing that neither needs nor could have a cause.

Some critics cling to the objection. They say there is no significant difference between ‘whatever goes from potential to actual has a cause’ and ‘everything has a cause’. That, Feser says, is as silly as saying there is no significant difference between ‘all triangles have three sides’ and ‘all geometrical figures have three sides’.

Others say the careful formulation is an ad hoc dodge invented to escape the objection. Three problems: (1) even if it were, that wouldn’t show the principle false — judging a claim by the motives of the person making it is an **ad hominem fallacy**; (2) it is **historically false** — for over 2,300 years, from Aristotle through Aquinas to today, defenders of the argument have always stated the principle this way; (3) there is nothing ad hoc about it — it flows naturally from Aristotle’s **analysis of change**, independently of any theistic argument, and you don’t need to believe in God to find it implausible that a mere potential could actualize itself. The only thing ad hoc here is the critics’ attempt to rescue an objection aimed at a straw man.

summary.heading: Hume and Kant on causation
summary.body:
**Hume.** Couldn’t a coffee cup or stone simply pop into existence uncaused? Hume thought this conceivable, and if it is, perhaps something could go from potential to actual without an actualizer. Feser replies in three ways.

- **Imagining is not conceiving an uncaused thing.** What Hume pictures is an empty space in which a stone suddenly appears. That is imaginable, but it is only conceiving of the stone *without also conceiving of* its cause — not conceiving of it as *having no* cause. You can conceive of a trilateral (a closed plane figure with three straight sides) without thinking of it as a triangle, yet no trilateral can exist without being a triangle. You can think of a man without thinking of his height, yet no man exists with no height. Conceiving of A without conceiving of B is not conceiving of A existing without B.
- **Anscombe’s point.** Hume must say why a cup suddenly appearing counts as *coming into existence* rather than merely being *transported* from elsewhere. The only way to tell those apart is by their **causes** — being molded from porcelain versus being carried in. So spelling out Hume’s scenario brings the notion of cause right back in.
- **The empirical evidence runs the other way.** It is ironic for an empiricist to doubt a principle so well confirmed by experience. When we look for causes we find them, and when we don’t (as with an unsolved murder) we have reason to think they’re there. If the principle were false, as W. Norris Clarke notes, nothing would be needed to produce anything — elephants or hotels could appear on your lawn, and should be doing so all the time. They aren’t. The best explanation is that there is something in the nature of potentiality that requires actualization by the actual. Otherwise the orderly world we observe would be miraculous.

**Kant.** Even granting causality within experience, why think it applies beyond experience, to something immaterial and unobservable? Feser answers that we conclude things need causes not **because we experience them** but **because they are merely potential until made actual**. The principle that no potential actualizes itself is fully general. Compare Euclidean geometry: we learn it from diagrams usually drawn in black ink, but it applies to figures of any color or no color. Restricting causality to the observable is like restricting geometry to figures we can see.

summary.heading: Russell on causation
summary.body:
In ‘On the Notion of Cause’, Bertrand Russell argued that causality is an outdated relic: physics describes the world with differential equations relating events, and those equations mention no causes, just formulas. Feser offers four replies.

1. **It proves too much.** If absence from the equations shows something unreal, we must also eliminate ‘event’, ‘law’ and ‘explanation’ — notions Russell’s own argument needs. As Jonathan Schaffer quips, that is like saying mathematics has eliminated the variable because the word ‘variable’ never appears in equations.
2. **Physics isn’t actually free of causal notions.** C. B. Martin argues that fundamental particles have **dispositional properties** — tendencies to produce certain effects in certain interactions.
3. **Other sciences plainly use causation**, and it is widely acknowledged that they can’t be reduced to physics — the social sciences, biology, and arguably chemistry. If they yield real knowledge, causation is real. Moreover, the naturalism underpinning modern atheism is usually defended with **causal** theories of knowledge, perception and meaning, so naturalists themselves are committed to causation.
4. **Most basically, physics is not an exhaustive description of reality.** The later Russell himself admitted that physics gives only the abstract, mathematical structure of events and is silent on their intrinsic nature — on what changes and what it changes from and to. Physics deliberately confines itself to what can be mathematically described (Martin calls it a ‘partial consideration’ of nature). That is the secret of its predictive power, but it guarantees physics will miss whatever isn’t mathematically capturable. Inferring from physics’ success that it describes everything is like inferring from metal detectors’ success that nothing nonmetallic exists; or a student taking only easy courses concluding other subjects contain nothing worth learning; or a drunk who finds things under the streetlamp concluding his keys can’t be anywhere else.

Since equations are mere abstractions, something must make the world actually conform to *these* equations rather than others or none — an intrinsic character in things. And if what the equations describe is really change, it is actualization of potential, which just is causation. Even someone who denies change in mind-independent reality must admit it in our **experiences** (setting up an experiment, then observing the result), which supply the evidence for physics; and the later Russell granted we know the physical world only because it **causally** affects our senses. So there’s no coherent way to use physics against causation.

summary.heading: Newton on inertia
summary.body:
Newton’s first law says a body in motion stays in motion unless acted on by an outside force. Doesn’t that show change can occur without a cause? Feser gives three replies (and points to a longer treatment in his essay ‘Motion in Aristotle, Newton, and Einstein’).

1. **Wrong question.** Newton’s law concerns events ordered in time — molecules swirling in a coffee cup. The argument is ultimately about what actualizes a thing’s potential to **exist** at a given moment — what makes the components of a water molecule constitute a water molecule right now. Newton’s law presupposes the existence of such things, so it cannot explain it.
2. **Laws presuppose natures.** Talk of a ‘law of nature’ is shorthand for how a thing tends to behave given its nature or form (a point defended later in the book). So what makes it the case that there are things with *that* nature — governed by inertia rather than some other law? What actualizes that potential? Newtonian mechanics can’t say.
3. **Mathematical abstraction.** Physics abstracts from whatever can’t be mathematized, including actuality, potentiality and so causation in the Aristotelian sense. Drawing on the historian James Weisheipl, Feser notes that the inertial principle isn’t proved by mathematical physics but *assumed* by it: to write equations, the mathematician must treat uniform motion and rest as the baseline needing no explanation and attend only to *changes* in them, which alone have quantitative value. Newton simply set aside the question of physical causes and sought quantities that could be equated. Such physics can neither affirm nor deny causal realities.

So Newtonian mechanics not only does not refute the principle of causality — it **could not**, any more than the drunk under the streetlamp can report on the rest of the street. However inertia is interpreted, it must be squared with the principle of causality, which reaches deeper than physics.

A long footnote adds that Aquinas held some motions follow **‘spontaneously’** from a substance’s nature, without a continuously conjoined external mover; their efficient cause is whatever generated the substance and gave it its form. Aquinas tied this to the now-discarded idea of natural places, but the general thesis is separable, and some contemporary Aristotelians read inertia this way: as the way a body tends to move given its nature.

summary.heading: Einstein and change
summary.body:
Some say Einstein — or rather Hermann Minkowski’s interpretation of relativity — showed change is illusory. On the **four-dimensional block universe** model, time is like space: just as distant places are as real as nearby ones, past and future moments are as real as the present. Nothing is really actualized; our sense that the present slides into the past is just how consciousness presents things.

This view is controversial even among physicists, but Feser doesn’t need to settle it, for two reasons.

1. **Incoherence.** Physics, relativity included, rests on observation and experiment — making a prediction, then testing it, moving from ignorance to knowledge. All of that is change. So denying change altogether undercuts the evidence for the very theory used to deny it; philosopher of science Richard Healey makes this point. At most one could say change exists only in the mind. But change in the mind is still actualization of potential, and that is all the argument needs to get started.
2. **Existence still needs actualizing.** Even if there were no change anywhere, the argument shows that a thing’s very **existence** at a moment involves actualized potential. So the block universe as a whole, existing as a single timeless whole, would still need an actualizer distinct from it — a cause of *this* sort of world being actual rather than some other. The same goes for a changeless mind.

So relativity at most affects **how** we apply the principle of causality, not **whether** we must apply it.

summary.heading: Quantum mechanics (1): indeterminism, Bell, and the vacuum
summary.body:
Three objections appeal to quantum mechanics: (a) quantum **indeterminism** conflicts with the principle of causality; (b) the **Bell inequalities** show there are correlations between distant measurements with no causal explanation; (c) quantum field theory shows **particles popping in and out of existence** at random.

First replies:

- **Indeterminism.** Some point out that the de Broglie–Bohm ‘hidden variable’ interpretation makes quantum mechanics deterministic. But the deeper Aristotelian point is that **causality does not entail determinism**. A cause need not necessitate its effect; it needs only to make it **intelligible**. And even on the indeterministic Copenhagen interpretation, as Robert Koons notes, every transition has causal antecedents — the prior wave state, or the prior wave state plus the measurement.
- **Bell.** Various responses have been proposed: allowing faster-than-light causal influence, backward causation, an absolute reference frame, or a law that the correlations obtain.
- **Vacuum fluctuations.** Alexander Pruss suggests either a hidden-variable theory or treating the system described by quantum field theory as the (indeterministic) cause of the events.

All such proposals raise questions — quantum interpretation is notoriously contested. But Feser’s main point lies deeper.

summary.heading: Quantum mechanics (2): absence from the map is not absence from the territory
summary.body:
The deeper point repeats the lesson from Newton. Mathematical physics, by its method, leaves out the qualitative and causal content of nature; it can neither affirm nor deny it. That is as true of quantum mechanics as of Newtonian mechanics. So if quantum theory assigns no cause to some event, it doesn’t follow that there is none: even a **completed** physics couldn’t capture every aspect of reality.

**The absence of something from a representation of nature is not a representation of its absence from nature.** And if we know in advance that the representation would omit it even if it were there, the omission doesn’t even make its absence *likely*. An artist’s black-and-white line drawing of a scene contains no color, but that doesn’t show the scene has none; the colorlessness is an artifact of the method. Likewise, mathematicization inherently drains out potentiality and hence causality. Quantum mechanics is something like a **limiting case** of this; the block universe is another. Drawing conclusions about causality from them mistakes abstractions for concrete reality. So these objections are not even well-formulated.

Feser adds that quantum mechanics may even **point toward** Aristotle. In comic-book art, a **color hold** is a contour left out of the black ink line art and supplied only by the color added later. Someone looking at the uncolored line art could still infer, from the lines and shadows that are there, where the missing edges of, say, a cube must go. Quantum theory may be like line art awaiting a color hold: its lines suggest the causality they don’t depict. Werner Heisenberg himself suggested that the probabilistic tendencies of quantum theory resemble Aristotle’s *potentia*, and that physicists had come to treat electron orbits as a kind of potentiality rather than full reality.

So: insofar as quantum theory depicts potentials being actualized **without depicting an actualizer**, it approximates **potentiality without actuality**. The block universe depicts **actuality without potentiality**. Causation requires both, so each picture leaves causation out — not because it is missing from reality, but because a thoroughly mathematicized description is bound to omit it. Finally, quantum objections appeal to laws of physics, and laws describe how things behave given their natures; so what makes it the case that there are things with *these* natures, obeying *these* laws? What actualizes that potential?

summary.heading: Quantum mechanics (3): radioactive decay
summary.body:
Radioactive decay is usually considered indeterministic and so a challenge to causality. Philosopher of science Phil Dowe offers an example: an unstable lead-210 atom may, without outside interference, decay into mercury-206, with some probability *x* of doing so in the next minute.

On the Aristotelian view, lead-210 simply behaves, as every natural thing does, according to its **nature or form**. Copper conducts electricity, a tree sinks roots, a dog chases squirrels — and lead-210 is the kind of thing that has probability *x* of decaying in the next minute. The decay is not deterministic, but it is not unintelligible; it is grounded in **what it is to be lead-210**. That is its **formal cause**. There is also an **efficient cause** that generated the atom in the first place. And most importantly, there is a deeper efficient cause of whatever keeps the atom **in existence here and now**: that something exists now as a lead-210 atom, with its indeterministic tendency to decay, rather than as something else or not at all, is itself an actualized potential, which needs an actualizer. So decay doesn’t remove the need for a purely actual actualizer; it just shows some causal situations are more complex than others. (A footnote compares this to Aquinas’ ‘spontaneous’ natural motions.)

Dowe himself reinforces the point. If I bring a bucket of lead-210 into a room and you get radiation sickness, I am obviously responsible — but I can’t be morally responsible for what I’m not causally responsible for. If only deterministic links count as causal, I’d be off the hook, which is absurd. And scientists themselves speak of decay as the **production** of mercury-206, and ‘production’ is nearly a synonym for ‘causation’. It sounds paradoxical only if you confuse deterministic causation with causation as such.

summary.heading: Outdated science?
summary.body:
Some claim that arguments like this rest on outdated science. One version is a sweeping assertion: modern science refuted Aristotelianism, so an Aristotelian proof of God is as obsolete as Aristotelian astronomy. Feser calls this intellectually sloppy. ‘Aristotelianism’ labels a huge range of scientific, philosophical, theological and political ideas. Certain **scientific** claims associated with medieval Aristotelianism — geocentrism, the four elements, natural places — have indeed been refuted. But the thesis that change is the actualization of potential is **metaphysical**, not scientific, and nothing in modern science refutes it. Indeed, since science presupposes change (observation and experiment involve going from one perceptual experience to another), any possible scientific theory presupposes actualization of potential. A later chapter develops how science rests on metaphysical foundations only philosophy can justify — and it is on those deeper foundations, not on revisable scientific claims, that the book’s arguments rest.

A second version targets the **examples**. Physicist Arthur Eddington famously contrasted the common-sense table — solid, extended — with the scientific table, a cloud of particles in mostly empty space; objects ‘rest’ on it because particles keep striking one another. So isn’t the desk-holding-the-cup example scientifically naïve? Feser finds this silly for three reasons.

- It assumes common sense and physics **compete**, which is controversial at best. That desk and cup are made of colliding particles doesn’t show the desk doesn’t really hold up the cup; it just describes the **mechanism** by which it does.
- The objection is raised **selectively**. Nobody accuses a structural engineer (on how thick a foundation must be to support a building) or a doctor (on a herniated disk failing to support the spine) of outdated science for ignoring particle physics.
- Most deeply, the scientific details are **irrelevant** to the point of the examples, which was to introduce actualization of potential and the linear/hierarchical distinction. Those notions apply whether we speak of desks holding cups or clouds of particles colliding. The details affect **how** we apply them, not **whether** we must. No one objects to a physicist’s thought experiment about riding a beam of light or falling into a black hole that photons are too small to sit on or that you’d be torn apart first. Such pedantry misses the point — and so does the Eddington objection.

summary.heading: Are hierarchical causal series real?
summary.body:
One more scientific worry: are there really causes that are simultaneous with their effects? We say a stick and the stone it pushes move together, but wouldn’t precise measurement reveal a slight time lag — likewise between the particles of the desk and the cup? And doesn’t relativity undermine simultaneity anyway?

- **Simultaneous doesn’t mean instantaneous.** An event like pushing a stone takes time, but the stick’s moving the stone and the stone’s being moved are aspects of **one and the same event**, however long it lasts. As Clarke puts it (with a different example), it takes time to push a chair across a room, but there is no time gap between the pushing and the chair’s being pushed.
- **Immediate causes are simultaneous with their effects.** Hume held causes always precede effects, but Stephen Mumford and Rani Lill Anjum show his standard examples fail. Billiard ball A’s earlier motion doesn’t strictly cause B’s motion — A might have been stopped short, and B may keep moving whether or not A remains. The causation happens at **impact**, and A’s impacting B and B’s being impacted are one event. Likewise, it is the brick’s pressing into the glass, not the earlier throw, that immediately causes the glass to give way. Earlier events are causally relevant, but they are not the **immediate** causes.
- **No collapse into one giant simultaneous event.** Distinguish causal episodes *within* a single process from separate processes that set up conditions for later ones. Mumford and Anjum’s example: sugar dissolving in tea, the tea being drunk ten minutes later, and the tea then being converted to energy in the stomach. Each is a causal process, but the dissolving doesn’t cause the drinking in the way water and the sugar’s structure cause the dissolving; it just sets up conditions. So there’s no absurd implication that all causal chains are simultaneous.
- **Relativity is irrelevant**, because the cases concern an immediate cause and effect that are parts of the same event at the same place, whereas relativity of simultaneity concerns spatially separated, distinct events.
- **Anyway, simultaneity isn’t the point.** The act–potency distinction applies to a thing’s very existence at any instant — the water’s atoms constituting water rather than separate hydrogen and oxygen. And what makes a series hierarchical is not simultaneity but **derivative, instrumental causal power**.

summary.heading: Why a hierarchical series can’t regress forever — and two misfiring objections
summary.body:
Because each member of a **linear** series has its causal power inherently (relative to the other members), no member’s action need be traced to a first member, so the series needn’t have a beginning. A footnote makes this vivid: Al begets Bob, who begets Chuck. Bob can beget Chuck whether or not Al is still alive; it is Bob, not Al using Bob as a tool, who begets Chuck. Yet in another sense none of them has inherent causal power *full stop*: none could beget or do anything for an instant unless the atoms and particles of their bodies were being actualized here and now as constituents of a body — and that is not in their power. Every stage of a linear series presupposes hierarchical ones.

In a **hierarchical** series, by contrast, each member except the first acts only insofar as power is imparted to it from outside. If D is actualized by C only as C is actualized by B, and B by A, then until we reach something that can actualize the rest without being actualized, we have explained nothing — we have just **passed the explanatory buck**. A hierarchical series with no first member would be like an instrument that is the instrument of nothing. Even if the series were infinitely long, a source of power **outside** it would still be needed. An infinitely long brush handle still couldn’t move itself; its length is irrelevant. Or picture a mirror reflecting the image of a face in another mirror, which reflects another, and so on forever: there must still be an actual **face** somewhere outside the series. You can’t have mirror images all the way down.

This disposes of two objections:

- **Infinite mathematical series** (e.g. Graham Oppy’s claim that Aquinas gives no reason to rule out an infinite regress) miss the point: they involve no instrumental and primary causes, indeed no causality at all. Aristotelians don’t rule out infinite series as such — they allow infinite mathematical series and even beginningless linear causal series. That is also why beginningless-multiverse cosmologies miss the point.
- **Begging the question** (a charge Feser finds in Jordan Howard Sobel): doesn’t calling causes ‘instrumental’ presuppose a first member? No. Calling something instrumental means only that its causal power is derived from something else. That doesn’t by itself assume the series can’t be infinite or that some cause has underived power. Even a skeptic understands that a stick can’t move a stone under its own power, whether or not he agrees that the regress must end.

summary.heading: Why an unmovable mover?
summary.body:
Grant that the argument reaches an **unmoved** mover. Does it reach an **unmovable** one — a first actualizer that is *purely* actual? Why not a first actualizer with potentials that just aren’t being actualized while it acts as first cause (perhaps actualized at other times, perhaps never)? Such a thing would lack unity, immateriality, eternity, perfection and omnipotence.

Feser’s reply recalls that the argument is ultimately about the actualizers of **existence**. The first actualizer is first because it actualizes the existence of other things **without its own existence needing actualization**. Suppose it had some potential that needed actualizing for it to exist. What actualizes it?

- **Something else?** Then this so-called first actualizer isn’t first after all; the other thing (or something beyond it) is.
- **A purely actual part of itself?** Then *that part* is the true first actualizer, and the potential ‘part’ is really just its first effect.
- **A part that is a mix of act and potency?** Then what actualizes that part’s potentials? Another mixed part? We’re back in a vicious regress with no first actualizer.

So there is no sense in a first actualizer of existence that isn’t purely actual. Acknowledge a first actualizer at all, and you acknowledge one with all the divine attributes that follow from pure actuality.

A final objection: anything that actualizes another thing must itself change in doing so, so a purely actual actualizer is **incoherent**. Feser has three replies.

1. **Begging the question.** The argument claims to prove that no potential could be actualized without a purely actual first actualizer. If its premises are true and its logic valid, the conclusion is true and hence coherent. The critic must show a false premise or an invalid step, not simply insist the conclusion is impossible. Otherwise the argument shows that a purely actual actualizer is possible, since it is actual.
2. **Fallacy of accident.** In our experience, things change others by changing themselves — your arm moves the stick by moving. But it doesn’t follow that *anything whatsoever* that actualizes must itself be actualized. That’s like reasoning that because every U.S. president has been under seven feet tall, no one who could ever be president could be seven feet tall. The connection is merely contingent, even if biology makes a seven-foot president unlikely. Likewise, nothing shows an *essential* link between being an actualizer and being a mix of act and potency.
3. **No contradiction, and a reason why ours change.** A ‘purely actual actualizer’ is not self-contradictory like an ‘immortal mortal’, something that both dies and doesn’t. It is just something that actualizes without being actualized. Indeed, the actualizers we know need to be actualized as they act **precisely because they are limited** — an arm is actually here and only potentially there, so its potential to be there must be actualized for it to move the stick there. Pure actuality has no such limits and so needs no actualizing as it acts.

Feser closes by noting that objections to first-cause arguments in general await a later chapter, but that the objections to the specifically Aristotelian argument all fail.
